patterns.name: Problem Classification
keywords: You do not know where to start
The input size rules out checking every possibility
Sorted data, repeated queries, or relationships suggest a structure
patterns.coreIdea: Before choosing an algorithm, ask what the input looks like, how large it can be, and what the answer must contain. Use those facts to narrow down the approaches worth trying.

patterns.name: Complexity Analysis
keywords: Need to compare two possible solutions
The straightforward solution times out
Preprocessing may make later queries cheaper
patterns.coreIdea: Count how the work and extra memory grow as the input grows. Include sorting, helper structures, recursion, and repeated queries, not just the main loop.

patterns.name: Invariant Design
keywords: Pointers divide processed and unprocessed items
An in-place update might overwrite needed information
A loop seems right but is hard to explain or prove
patterns.coreIdea: Write down what must remain true while the algorithm runs. Use that rule to decide which pointer moves, swaps, or updates are safe.

patterns.name: State Design
keywords: Future choices depend on earlier choices
A DP or visited key needs more than an index
Many different paths lead to the same remaining problem
patterns.coreIdea: Keep exactly the information needed to make the next decision. If two histories with the same saved state can have different futures, the state is missing something.

patterns.name: Reduction
keywords: A story hides a graph, interval, or subset problem
A difficult objective can become a yes/no check
Changing the representation makes a known algorithm applicable
patterns.coreIdea: Rewrite the problem as one you already know how to solve. Check that the transformation keeps the original constraints and the meaning of the answer.

patterns.name: Greedy Thinking
keywords: Each choice reduces the remaining options
Choosing an early finish or smaller cost may preserve flexibility
Need a proof that a local choice is safe
patterns.coreIdea: Make the best immediate choice only when you can explain why it cannot block a better final answer. Try small counterexamples before trusting the rule.

patterns.name: Linear Scan
keywords: Each answer depends on the current item and a small summary
Need to detect a change between neighbors
Input can be processed as it arrives
patterns.coreIdea: Walk through the input once and update a small running summary, such as a count, previous value, or best answer so far.

patterns.name: Running Extremum and Kadane’s Algorithm
keywords: Need the best sum of a consecutive segment
An earlier minimum can give the best later gain
Keeping a harmful prefix makes the next candidate worse
patterns.coreIdea: For a maximum subarray sum, decide at each item whether to extend the previous segment or start a new one. Keep the best ending here and the best seen anywhere; other running-extremum problems keep a minimum or maximum seen earlier.

patterns.name: Frequency Counting
keywords: Need duplicate detection or occurrence counts
Compare or group anagrams
Need to find a matching value seen earlier
patterns.coreIdea: Use a table to count how often each value appears. Look up those counts instead of repeatedly scanning the input; for a pair target, a table can also remember earlier values.

patterns.name: In-Place Index Marking
keywords: Values fit a known range of array indices
Need missing or duplicate values with little extra memory
A matrix can reuse its first row and column as markers
patterns.coreIdea: Reuse the input array as a record of what has been seen, often by marking the position associated with a value. Only do this when mutation is allowed and the original information can still be recovered when needed.

patterns.name: Cyclic Placement
keywords: Values belong to a range such as 1 through n
Need a missing or repeated value
Array may be rearranged and values map to target indices
patterns.coreIdea: When each value has a designated array position, swap it toward that position. Stop when it is placed, out of range, or would only swap with a duplicate.

patterns.name: Prefix Sum
keywords: Many sum queries on unchanged input
Count consecutive segments with a given sum
Negative numbers make a simple shrinking sum window unsuitable
patterns.coreIdea: Save the sum before each position. Get a range sum by subtracting two saved totals; for counting target-sum subarrays, count earlier prefixes with the required difference.

patterns.name: Prefix XOR
keywords: Need XOR of many consecutive ranges
Pairs of equal values should cancel
A substring rule depends on odd or even character counts
patterns.coreIdea: Save cumulative XOR values. XOR two prefixes to cancel everything before a range; for odd/even count rules, toggle bits to represent parity.

patterns.name: Prefix/Suffix Decomposition
keywords: Need an answer excluding the current element
Each position depends on both earlier and later values
Need to evaluate many possible split points
patterns.coreIdea: Make one pass from the left and one from the right, saving the information each side contributes. Combine the two sides to answer a question about an index or split.

patterns.name: Difference Array
keywords: Many additions over intervals before reading final values
Need accumulated bookings, passengers, or coverage
Processing every element of every update would be too slow
patterns.coreIdea: For an inclusive range addition, add the change at its start and subtract it just after its end. After all updates, a running sum reconstructs the value at every position.

patterns.name: Coordinate Compression
keywords: Coordinates are huge but only a few are used
Need array indices for a Fenwick or segment tree
Only comparisons and ranks matter, or original gaps can be stored separately
patterns.coreIdea: Sort the distinct coordinates and replace each with its position in that order. This preserves order and equality, but not physical distances or gaps.

patterns.name: Matrix Traversal and Direction Simulation
keywords: Visit cells in spiral or diagonal order
Simulate turns or movement on a grid
Rotate, reshape, or process matrix layers
patterns.coreIdea: Track the current row, column, and movement rule explicitly. Use direction steps for movement and shrinking boundaries or layers for spiral traversal and rotation.

patterns.name: Opposite-Direction Two Pointers
keywords: Find a pair in sorted input
Compare characters from both ends
Discarding one endpoint can be justified from the current comparison
patterns.coreIdea: Start two pointers at opposite ends. Use sorted order or a matching rule to decide which end can be safely discarded; the movement rule depends on the problem.

patterns.name: Same-Direction Two Pointers
keywords: Remove values in place while preserving order
Compact nonzero or distinct values at the front
Check whether one sequence appears in another in the same order
patterns.coreIdea: Move a reading pointer forward while another pointer tracks where to write or what to match next. Keep the already processed part valid as both advance.

patterns.name: Fast-Slow Pointer
keywords: A linked list may contain a cycle
Repeated value-to-index jumps form a hidden cycle
Need a midpoint without first counting all nodes
patterns.coreIdea: Follow the same next-step rule with one slow and one fast pointer. Different speeds reveal a cycle or midpoint; a fixed gap is a related technique for positions measured from the end.

patterns.name: Expand Around Center
keywords: Need a palindromic substring rather than a subsequence
A substring grows by matching both ends
Input size allows checking every center
patterns.coreIdea: Try every character and every gap as a palindrome center. Move outward while both sides match, checking odd and even lengths; this approach is quadratic in the worst case.

patterns.name: Dutch National Flag / Three-Way Partitioning
keywords: Only three value classes such as 0, 1, and 2
Need an in-place partition around a pivot
The unclassified region shrinks after each decision
patterns.coreIdea: Keep regions for small, equal, large, and not-yet-classified values. Move each unknown value to its region; after a swap from the right, inspect the arriving value before advancing.

patterns.name: Fixed Sliding Window
keywords: Every candidate has the same length
Need a rolling sum or character count
Repeatedly recomputing each fixed-size block is too slow
patterns.coreIdea: Keep exactly k consecutive items. Add the incoming item and remove the outgoing item as the window moves; record an answer only after a full window exists.

patterns.name: Variable Sliding Window
keywords: Need the longest or shortest consecutive section
Counts or positive sums give a predictable shrinking rule
Items can enter on the right and leave on the left without revisiting them
patterns.coreIdea: Keep a consecutive section and move its right end to add items. Move its left end when needed: shrink until valid for longest-window problems, or record and shrink while valid for shortest-window problems. This needs a rule that supports one-way boundary movement.

patterns.name: Monotonic Queue
keywords: Need a maximum or minimum in every moving window
Older candidates expire
A newer candidate can be proved at least as useful as an older one
patterns.coreIdea: Keep candidate indices in a deque. Remove expired candidates at the front and candidates made useless by a newer value at the back; the front then gives the current best candidate.

patterns.name: Sort + Scan
keywords: Equal or related values should be grouped
Comparing neighbors would solve the problem after sorting
Reordering input is allowed or can be done on a copy
patterns.coreIdea: Sort the items so useful relationships become visible between neighbors or in a single pass. Include the sorting cost and keep original indices if the answer needs them.

patterns.name: Sort + Greedy
keywords: Need to select non-overlapping tasks or make ordered assignments
An early finish or suitable size leaves more options
Reordering is allowed and the greedy rule can be justified
patterns.coreIdea: Choose a sort order that exposes a safe greedy decision, then process items in that order. The sort key needs a correctness argument, such as preserving more room for future choices.

patterns.name: Merge-Sort Counting
keywords: Count inversions or smaller values to the right
A pair must satisfy both an index order and a value comparison
Sorted halves make cross-pair counting faster
patterns.coreIdea: Split the input by original position, sort both halves, and count qualifying cross-half pairs before merging. Two moving boundaries can replace checking every pair separately.

patterns.name: Quickselect / Partition Selection
keywords: Need kth smallest or largest in unsorted input
Do not need the entire array sorted
Partitioning or mutating the input is acceptable
patterns.coreIdea: Partition around a pivot, then continue only on the side containing the requested rank. Random pivots give expected linear time, but ordinary quickselect can still take quadratic time in the worst case.

patterns.name: Sweep Line
keywords: Count overlapping intervals
Compute a skyline, covered length, or area
The answer changes only at object boundaries
patterns.coreIdea: Turn starts, ends, or geometric boundaries into ordered events. Move across them while updating what is currently active; decide carefully how events at the same coordinate are ordered.

patterns.name: Event Processing
keywords: Tasks arrive and finish at different times
Resources become available after earlier work ends
Equal-time events need explicit tie-breaking
patterns.coreIdea: Process arrivals, completions, and other changes in time order. Keep pending events or available resources in suitable queues or heaps, and jump over times when nothing happens.

patterns.name: Classic Binary Search
keywords: Find an exact value in sorted data
Random access to the middle is cheap
Each comparison can rule out half the remaining positions
patterns.coreIdea: In sorted input, compare the middle value with the target and discard the half that cannot contain it. Use one boundary convention consistently so every step makes progress.

patterns.name: Lower Bound
keywords: Need the leftmost matching value
Need an insertion position before equal values
Count how many sorted values are below a threshold
patterns.coreIdea: Find the first position whose value is at least the target. Keep moving the boundary left on equality; the result can be the position just after the array.

patterns.name: Upper Bound
keywords: Need the boundary after repeated equal values
Count sorted values at most a threshold
Find the last value at or below a limit
patterns.coreIdea: Find the first position whose value is greater than the target. Move past equality; subtract one for a possible last matching position, then check it before using it.

patterns.name: Binary Search on Answer
keywords: Smallest workable speed, capacity, or time
Largest minimum distance that can be achieved
A candidate answer is easier to check than to construct directly
patterns.coreIdea: Guess a candidate answer and test whether it is feasible. If feasibility changes in only one direction as the guess increases, search for the first or last feasible value; include the test cost in the runtime.

patterns.name: Parametric Search
keywords: Need an approximate numeric answer
Feasibility changes only once as a threshold changes
The cost lies mainly in checking each candidate parameter
patterns.coreIdea: Express the objective as a parameter and build a monotonic yes/no test. Search its transition; integer parameters need exact boundary rules, while real-valued parameters need a justified precision or iteration limit.

patterns.name: Stack Simulation and Cancellation
keywords: An operation affects the most recent item
Adjacent values cancel or merge
Need backspace, undo, or collision simulation
patterns.coreIdea: Keep unresolved items in a stack. Compare each new item with the most recent unresolved item, then push, combine, cancel, or pop according to the rule.

patterns.name: Parentheses Matching
keywords: Check nested brackets or scopes
Need to identify unmatched opening or closing symbols
Count insertions, removals, or nesting depth
patterns.coreIdea: Keep unmatched opening brackets in a stack. Each closing bracket must match the latest opener; for a single bracket type, a balance counter may be enough.

patterns.name: Expression Evaluation
keywords: An expression contains operators and parentheses
Multiplication must happen before addition
Input is postfix notation or follows a small expression grammar
patterns.coreIdea: Keep track of values and operators, applying operations in the required precedence order. Use stacks or recursive parsing to handle parentheses and nested expressions.

patterns.name: Monotonic Increasing Stack
keywords: Find previous or next smaller values
Count each value's contribution as a subarray minimum
Remove larger earlier digits while preserving order
patterns.coreIdea: Keep candidate indices in increasing value order. When a smaller value arrives, pop larger candidates whose next-smaller boundary or usefulness is now decided; equal values need a deliberate tie rule.

patterns.name: Monotonic Decreasing Stack
keywords: Find the next warmer day or larger value
Measure a span bounded by a greater value
Earlier candidates wait for a larger item
patterns.coreIdea: Keep candidate indices in decreasing value order. When a larger value arrives, pop smaller candidates whose next-greater answer is now known; decide explicitly how to handle equal values.

patterns.name: Histogram and Maximal Rectangle
keywords: Largest rectangle under a histogram
Largest all-one rectangle in a matrix
Rectangle width is limited by the nearest smaller heights
patterns.coreIdea: Treat each histogram bar as the shortest bar of a possible rectangle. Find how far it can extend before a smaller bar blocks it; for a binary matrix, build a histogram of consecutive ones for each row.

patterns.name: Top K with a Heap
keywords: Need k largest, smallest, or most frequent items
Values arrive as a stream
Sorting all candidates would do unnecessary work
patterns.coreIdea: Keep only the best k candidates in a heap. Put the weakest retained candidate at the root so a better incoming item can replace it cheaply.

patterns.name: Two Heaps
keywords: Need a median while values arrive
Need to maintain a changing rank boundary
Can keep two ordered groups balanced after updates
patterns.coreIdea: Split values into a lower half and an upper half. Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balancing their sizes so the middle values stay available.

patterns.name: K-Way Merge
keywords: Merge several already sorted lists or streams
Need the next smallest item across sorted sources
Need only an early prefix or kth merged value
patterns.coreIdea: Put the next available item from each sorted source in a heap. Remove the smallest item, then add only the next item from the source it came from.

patterns.name: Heap Scheduling
keywords: Choose the next available server or task
Release times, deadlines, or cooldowns matter
The best eligible choice changes as events occur
patterns.coreIdea: Use a heap to choose among tasks or resources that are currently available. Process release or completion times in order, and encode the problem's exact priority and tie rules.

patterns.name: Heap with Lazy Deletion
keywords: Priorities change after insertion
Items leave a moving window
Need deletion that the heap interface does not support directly
patterns.coreIdea: When a heap entry becomes outdated, mark it invalid elsewhere instead of searching the heap to remove it. Skip stale entries when they reach the top; periodic cleanup may be needed if stale entries accumulate.

patterns.name: Dummy Node
keywords: The head can be inserted, deleted, or replaced
Building a result list needs a stable starting point
Repeated special handling for the first node complicates the code
patterns.coreIdea: Place a temporary node before the real list head. This gives every real node a predecessor, so changing the first node uses the same logic as changing a later one.

patterns.name: Linked-List Reversal
keywords: Reverse a list or part of it
Reorder a list using a reversed second half
Need to change links in place without losing the remaining nodes
patterns.coreIdea: Before changing a node's next link, save the next node. Reverse the link toward the processed part, then advance until the required list or segment is reversed.

patterns.name: Reverse in K-Groups
keywords: Reverse linked-list nodes in fixed-size groups
Need to reconnect several reversed segments
The final group may be shorter than k
patterns.coreIdea: Check that the next k nodes exist, reverse that group, and reconnect it to the previous and remaining groups. Leave a shorter final group unchanged when the problem requires it.

patterns.name: Linked-List Fast-Slow Pointer
keywords: Split a list into halves
Find the middle in one pass
Find the nth node from the end without first counting nodes
patterns.coreIdea: Use a one-step and two-step pointer to locate the middle, or keep a fixed gap to locate a node relative to the end. Choose the starting positions to match the required middle or predecessor.

patterns.name: Linked-List Merge
keywords: Merge already sorted linked lists
Need to reuse nodes instead of copying values
Combining sorted halves during list merge sort
patterns.coreIdea: Compare the current nodes of sorted lists and link the smaller one to the output tail. Advance only that list, then attach the remaining suffix when one input ends.

patterns.name: Linked-List Cycle Detection
keywords: A list may never reach null
Need to detect a cycle without a visited set
Need the node where a cycle begins
patterns.coreIdea: Move one pointer one link and another two links until they meet or reach the end. A meeting proves a reachable cycle; moving one pointer back to the head then finds the entry by equal-speed steps.

patterns.name: Divide-and-Conquer List Sorting
keywords: Need to sort a linked list efficiently
Array-style random indexing is unavailable
A stable sort can be built from sorted-list merging
patterns.coreIdea: Split the list into two halves, sort each half, and merge the sorted lists by relinking nodes. Recursive merge sort uses a logarithmic call stack; bottom-up merging can avoid that stack.

patterns.name: Merge Intervals
keywords: Combine overlapping ranges
Insert a range into an already merged list
Need the union as disjoint intervals
patterns.coreIdea: Sort intervals by their start. Extend the current interval while the next one overlaps; when a gap appears, save the current result and start another. Check whether touching endpoints count as overlap.

patterns.name: Interval Scheduling
keywords: Select as many compatible intervals as possible
Remove the fewest intervals to eliminate overlap
Intervals have equal value and an early finish preserves future choices
patterns.coreIdea: For the maximum number of unweighted non-overlapping intervals, repeatedly choose the one that finishes earliest. Weighted jobs need DP or another method, not this same greedy rule.

patterns.name: Interval Partitioning
keywords: Minimum meeting rooms or parallel groups
Resources can be reused after an interval ends
Need the maximum number of concurrent intervals
patterns.coreIdea: Process intervals by start time. Reuse a resource when its previous interval has ended; otherwise allocate another. The minimum resource count equals the largest simultaneous overlap.

patterns.name: Exchange Argument
keywords: A local rule seems plausible but needs proof
Two neighboring choices can be exchanged
Need to show that some optimal solution begins with the greedy choice
patterns.coreIdea: To justify a greedy rule, take an optimal solution that differs from it and show that replacing the first differing choice cannot make the result worse.

patterns.name: Greedy + Heap
keywords: Need the best feasible subset rather than every item
An earlier choice may need to be replaced
The worst chosen duration, cost, or benefit must be found quickly
patterns.coreIdea: Combine a greedy processing order with a heap of choices. When constraints are exceeded or a better candidate appears, the heap identifies which current choice to remove or replace.

patterns.name: Greedy Reachability and Coverage
keywords: Minimum jumps to an endpoint
Cover a continuous target with few segments
Need to detect an unreachable gap
patterns.coreIdea: Track the farthest boundary reachable with the choices made so far. Among options starting before that boundary, choose the one extending it farthest; detect a gap when no option extends reach.

patterns.name: Tree DFS
keywords: A result depends on child subtrees
Need preorder, inorder, or postorder traversal
Depth or ancestor information belongs on the current path
patterns.coreIdea: Explore one child subtree fully before moving to the next. Decide what each call receives and returns, and whether to act before the children, between them, or after them.

patterns.name: Tree BFS
keywords: Need level order or the nearest leaf
Compute a maximum, average, or view for each level
Nodes at equal depth should be processed together
patterns.coreIdea: Use a queue to visit the tree one depth at a time. Process the current queue length as one level before adding the next level's results.

patterns.name: Binary Search Tree
keywords: Input is explicitly a binary search tree
Need successor, rank, or a value range
A comparison with the current key can discard one subtree
patterns.coreIdea: Use the rule that left-subtree keys come before the node and right-subtree keys come after it. This enables ordered search and sorted inorder traversal; duplicate handling depends on the tree's definition.

patterns.name: Divide-and-Conquer Tree Construction
keywords: Rebuild a tree from traversals
Construct a balanced tree from sorted values
A root divides an input range into smaller ranges
patterns.coreIdea: Identify the root from the input representation, split the remaining data into child subproblems, and build each recursively. Traversal reconstruction needs enough information; duplicates or a single traversal may make it ambiguous.

patterns.name: Root-to-Leaf Path State
keywords: Root-to-leaf sums or numbers
Need to list paths satisfying a rule
A node's answer depends on its ancestors
patterns.coreIdea: Carry a running value or path from the root into each child. Check it at the required node or leaf, and undo changes to a shared path list when returning.

patterns.name: Tree DP
keywords: Choose nodes under parent-child restrictions
Best answer combines independent child subtrees
Need an answer for every possible root
patterns.coreIdea: For each subtree, return the few results its parent needs, such as taking or skipping the root. Combine child results after visiting them; rerooting adds a pass for answers viewed from every root.

patterns.name: Tree Diameter
keywords: Find the farthest pair of nodes in a tree
Longest path may pass through a branching node
Need the tree diameter or center
patterns.coreIdea: For an unweighted tree, combine the two longest downward paths at each node to consider a path through it. Return only the longest downward path to its parent and keep the best full path separately.

patterns.name: Lowest Common Ancestor
keywords: Find where two root-to-node paths meet
Compute distances or paths between tree nodes
Many ancestor queries reuse the same tree
patterns.coreIdea: Find the deepest node that is an ancestor of both targets. One query can use a recursive search; many queries justify preprocessing ancestor jumps or a traversal-based index.

patterns.name: Tree Serialization
keywords: Save and restore a tree
Compare subtree shapes and values
Need a deterministic signature for repeated subtrees
patterns.coreIdea: Write both node values and enough structure information to rebuild the same tree. A traversal with explicit null markers is one option; values alone are generally insufficient.

patterns.name: Morris Traversal
keywords: Need inorder traversal without a stack or recursion
Temporary pointer changes are permitted
Must restore the tree after visiting it
patterns.coreIdea: Traverse a binary tree using temporary links back from an inorder predecessor. Remove each temporary link after returning so the original tree is restored; input mutation must be allowed.

patterns.name: Graph Modeling and Adjacency Representation
keywords: Objects are connected by relationships
Moves between configurations can be generated
Need to decide whether edges are directed or weighted
patterns.coreIdea: Turn objects into nodes and allowed relationships or moves into edges. Preserve direction and weight, then choose neighbor lists, a matrix, or on-demand neighbors to suit the graph.

patterns.name: Graph DFS
keywords: Need to find everything reachable from a node
Count connected regions
Explore a path deeply before returning
patterns.coreIdea: Explore one unvisited neighbor at a time and backtrack when none remain. Mark visited nodes to avoid repeating work; cycle detection needs extra state appropriate to directed or undirected edges.

patterns.name: Graph BFS
keywords: Fewest moves or edges in an unweighted graph
Find the nearest reachable target
Need level-by-level exploration
patterns.coreIdea: Use a queue to explore all nodes one edge away before those two edges away. First discovery gives a shortest path only when every move has equal cost.

patterns.name: Multi-Source BFS
keywords: Several starting points act simultaneously
Find distance to the nearest zero, exit, or facility
Model equal-speed spread or infection
patterns.coreIdea: Start one BFS with every source already in the queue at distance zero. The expanding waves give each cell or node its distance to the nearest source.

patterns.name: State-Space BFS
keywords: A position can be revisited with different keys or resources
Need the fewest operations to reach a configuration
A puzzle state includes more than location
patterns.coreIdea: Treat the full situation as a graph node, not just its position. Store every feature affecting future moves in the visited key, then BFS for the fewest equal-cost moves.

patterns.name: Topological Sort
keywords: Courses or tasks have prerequisites
Need a valid dependency order
Need to detect a directed cycle that blocks completion
patterns.coreIdea: Order tasks so each prerequisite comes before the tasks that depend on it. Repeatedly process tasks with no remaining prerequisites; if some never become available, a cycle prevents a full ordering.

patterns.name: Union Find / Disjoint Set Union
keywords: Connections are added over time
Need to merge accounts, regions, or equivalent items
Ask whether two elements belong to the same component
patterns.coreIdea: Keep elements in groups, each with a representative. Merge groups and compare representatives to test connectivity; this handles additions well, but ordinary union-find cannot undo arbitrary edge deletions.

patterns.name: Bipartite Coloring
keywords: Split items into two groups with no within-group conflict
Every edge requires opposite assignments
Need to check whether a graph is bipartite
patterns.coreIdea: Try assigning one of two colors to every node, giving neighbors opposite colors. A same-color edge is a conflict; for an undirected graph, this is equivalent to an odd cycle.

patterns.name: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
keywords: Shortest paths have nonnegative costs
Need minimum travel time or total cost
Choosing the nearest pending state can safely finalize it
patterns.coreIdea: Repeatedly expand the node with the smallest known distance and improve its neighbors through that node. Standard Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights; skip outdated heap entries.

patterns.name: 0–1 BFS
keywords: Moves are either free or cost one
Minimize changes or edge reversals
A graph has exactly two weights, zero and one
patterns.coreIdea: For edges costing only zero or one, use a deque: put improved zero-cost neighbors at the front and one-cost neighbors at the back. This keeps cheaper distances ahead without a heap.

patterns.name: Bellman–Ford
keywords: Negative edge weights are possible
Need to detect a reachable negative cycle
A path is limited to a fixed number of edges or stops
patterns.coreIdea: Repeatedly try improving distances through every edge. With no reachable negative cycle, n minus one full rounds suffice; a further improvement reveals one. For an edge-count limit, read the previous round's distances rather than reusing new ones immediately.

patterns.name: Floyd–Warshall
keywords: Many shortest-path queries between arbitrary pairs
The graph is small enough for a cubic-time method
Need all-pairs reachability or conversion costs
patterns.coreIdea: Keep a table for every source-destination pair. Allow one more intermediate node at a time and check whether going through it shortens each route; initialize self-distances to zero.

patterns.name: Minimum Spanning Tree
keywords: Need to connect every location at minimum total cost
The objective is total network cost, not a route from one source
Cycles add unnecessary cost to the required connection structure
patterns.coreIdea: Connect all vertices of an undirected weighted graph with the cheapest total edge cost and no cycles. Grow a tree with Prim or add cheapest safe edges with Kruskal; a disconnected graph gives a forest.

patterns.name: Subsets Backtracking
keywords: Generate all possible selections
Item order does not change the answer
Need unique subsets when values repeat
patterns.coreIdea: Build subsets by choosing or skipping each item. Undo each choice after exploring it; for duplicate input values, skip equivalent choices at the same decision depth.

patterns.name: Permutations Backtracking
keywords: Generate arrangements where order matters
Each item can be used once
Need all unique permutations
patterns.coreIdea: Fill positions one at a time using items not yet chosen. Undo each placement after exploring it; repeated values need duplicate-skipping or frequency counts.

patterns.name: Combinations Backtracking
keywords: Choose k items without caring about order
Find combinations reaching a target sum
Candidates may be single-use or reusable
patterns.coreIdea: Build combinations using a start index so the same selection is not generated in different orders. Advance past a chosen item for single use, or keep its index when reuse is allowed.

patterns.name: Constraint Search
keywords: Small input permits exploring many assignments
Partial choices can already violate a rule
Need an exact arrangement such as a board or schedule
patterns.coreIdea: Try one decision, check its constraints, and abandon the branch as soon as it cannot succeed. Undo the decision before trying another; bounds can also reject branches unable to beat the best answer.

patterns.name: Grid Path Backtracking
keywords: Spell a word or collect items along a grid path
The current path cannot reuse a cell
Future legal moves depend on the cells already used on that path
patterns.coreIdea: Try a legal move to a neighboring cell, mark it as used by the current path, then undo that mark when returning. Path-specific marking lets other candidate paths reuse the cell later.

patterns.name: Fibonacci DP
keywords: Ways to climb steps or tile a narrow strip
Each state depends on the previous one or two
A simple recurrence repeats the same smaller calculations
patterns.coreIdea: Write the answer at a position using a few earlier answers, then compute in order from correct base cases. When only the last few answers matter, replace the full table with a few variables.

patterns.name: Linear DP
keywords: Choices follow a sequence
Need a best answer up to each position
The same earlier subproblem is used by several later choices
patterns.coreIdea: Define what the best answer for a prefix or ending position means. Compute it from earlier states, choosing among valid transitions such as take, skip, or extend.

patterns.name: Grid DP
keywords: Count paths or minimize cost through a grid
Moves create an acyclic order such as right/down
Obstacles or budgets affect which transitions are allowed
patterns.coreIdea: Store an answer for each cell and compute it from allowed earlier neighbors. Add state for any extra resource, direction, or second traveler that changes future choices.

patterns.name: 0/1 Knapsack
keywords: Choose a subset under a weight or capacity limit
Each item is available at most once
Need exact subset-sum feasibility or maximum value
patterns.coreIdea: For each item, choose to take it once or skip it within the capacity limit. In a one-dimensional table, process capacities backward so the same item is not used again in that iteration.

patterns.name: Unbounded Knapsack
keywords: Each item or denomination is available repeatedly
Build an exact amount or length
Need minimum pieces, maximum value, or a count of constructions
patterns.coreIdea: Allow a chosen item to be used again when building a total. Forward capacity updates permit reuse; loop order must match whether order matters to the answer.

patterns.name: Coin Change
keywords: Make an amount from denominations
Reuse coins or respect per-coin limits
Distinguish counting ways from minimizing the number used
patterns.coreIdea: First decide whether the question asks for the fewest coins, unordered combinations, or ordered sequences. These use different recurrences or loop orders even though the state often tracks the amount.

patterns.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
keywords: Keep original order while selecting increasing values
Need minimum removals to obtain increasing order
A nesting problem can become increasing-subsequence search after careful sorting
patterns.coreIdea: For the longest strictly increasing subsequence, keep the smallest possible ending value for every length and replace the first ending value at least as large as the new item. This tails array gives the length, not necessarily the subsequence itself.

patterns.name: Longest Common Subsequence
keywords: Find the longest sequence shared in the same relative order
Matches need not be consecutive
Insertions or deletions can be related to a shared subsequence
patterns.coreIdea: Compare two prefixes. If their last elements match, extend the answer for the shorter prefixes; otherwise keep the better answer after skipping one last element.

patterns.name: Edit Distance
keywords: Need minimum edits between strings
Operations can insert, remove, or replace characters
Each decision aligns prefixes of two sequences
patterns.coreIdea: Build a table for converting one prefix into another. Compare the costs of insert, delete, replace, or match; initialize empty-prefix cases explicitly.

patterns.name: Interval DP
keywords: Operations join or remove neighboring groups
The first or last operation splits the remaining work
Need an optimal answer for every contiguous range
patterns.coreIdea: Define an answer for each interval. Choose a split or an operation inside it, combine answers for smaller intervals, and process short intervals before long ones.

patterns.name: Partition DP
keywords: Split a sequence into consecutive groups
Exactly k parts are required
Each segment has its own cost or validity rule
patterns.coreIdea: Choose where the last segment begins, combine its cost with the best answer before it, and try all valid cuts. Add the number of groups to the state when it is constrained.

patterns.name: State Machine DP
keywords: Only a few modes describe the relevant history
Buying and selling have restrictions
Certain consecutive actions are forbidden
patterns.coreIdea: Keep a separate DP value for each allowed mode, such as holding stock, resting, or cooling down. Update modes through legal transitions using the previous step's values.

patterns.name: Digit DP
keywords: Count integers in a large numeric range
Digits must satisfy a sum, repetition, or forbidden-pattern rule
Cannot enumerate every number individually
patterns.coreIdea: Count numbers one digit at a time, tracking whether the prefix still matches the upper bound and whether meaningful digits have started. Include whatever digit information the rule needs; count a range by subtracting two bounded counts.

patterns.name: Bitmask DP
keywords: Only a small number of items allows about 2^n states
Need to visit, assign, or group each item
Different choice orders lead to the same completed subset
patterns.coreIdea: Use the bits of an integer to record which items are already chosen or finished. Add another index or mode when the subset alone does not determine future choices.

patterns.name: Probability DP
keywords: Repeated random moves or trials
Need the chance of ending in a target state
Need an expected cost or number of steps with clearly defined stopping states
patterns.coreIdea: Store the probability of each situation and distribute it through the next random outcomes. For expected values, write the expectation recurrence separately rather than treating it as an ordinary probability table.

patterns.name: Game DP
keywords: Two players alternate choices
The opponent chooses the best response
Need a guaranteed win or optimal final score
patterns.coreIdea: Describe each state from the player whose turn it is. A winning move reaches a losing state for the opponent; score games often track the best score difference when both play optimally.

patterns.name: DAG DP
keywords: Count paths or find a longest path in a DAG
Tasks depend on completed prerequisite states
Sequence or grid DP generalizes to irregular directed connections
patterns.coreIdea: Compute each state after all the states it depends on. A directed acyclic graph provides a topological order; memoized recursion is another option when dependencies cannot cycle.

patterns.name: Trie
keywords: Need prefix lookup or autocomplete
Many dictionary words share starting characters
Need to choose bits for maximum-XOR matching
patterns.coreIdea: Store strings as paths of characters, sharing nodes for common prefixes. Follow a prefix once to reach all its possible completions; bit tries apply the same idea to binary digits.

patterns.name: Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP)
keywords: Find exact pattern occurrences in a long text
Matches can overlap
Need deterministic linear-time matching for one pattern
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute which shorter prefix of the pattern can still match after a mismatch. Fall back to that prefix instead of restarting and rechecking text characters already understood.

patterns.name: Z Algorithm
keywords: Need prefix-match lengths at every position
Find repeated prefix/suffix borders
Pattern matching can use pattern + separator + text
patterns.coreIdea: For each string position, record how many characters match the start of the string. Reuse a previously known matching interval rather than compare every prefix from scratch.

patterns.name: Rabin–Karp
keywords: Search fixed-length windows for a pattern
Many windows can be rejected by a short fingerprint
Hash collisions must be checked or accepted as a probabilistic trade-off
patterns.coreIdea: Slide a hash value over text windows of the pattern's length. A different hash rules a match out; an equal hash identifies a candidate that needs character verification for guaranteed correctness.

patterns.name: Rolling Hash
keywords: Many substring-equality comparisons
Find repeated or common substrings
Binary search needs a fast candidate-length check
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute hash totals and powers so a substring's fingerprint can be obtained quickly. Equal hashes do not prove equal substrings; direct checking guarantees correctness, while multiple hashes only reduce collision risk.

patterns.name: Manacher’s Algorithm
keywords: Need palindrome lengths for all centers
Quadratic center expansion is too slow
Need linear-time palindrome preprocessing
patterns.coreIdea: Track the farthest-reaching palindrome found so far. Reuse the known radius at a mirrored center, then compare characters only as needed beyond the known boundary; handle odd and even centers consistently.

patterns.name: Aho–Corasick
keywords: Search many dictionary patterns in one text
Need overlapping or streaming matches
Detect forbidden words or patterns efficiently
patterns.coreIdea: Build a trie of all patterns, then add fallback links to the longest suffix that is still a dictionary prefix. Follow these links while scanning text and report matching pattern endings, including suffix matches.

patterns.name: Suffix Array
keywords: Need lexicographic order of substrings
Find a longest repeated substring
Many substring searches reuse the same text
patterns.coreIdea: Sort the starting positions of all suffixes in dictionary order. Neighboring suffixes reveal shared prefixes; a longest-common-prefix array supports repeated-substring and distinct-substring questions.

patterns.name: Suffix Automaton
keywords: Count distinct substrings without listing them
Match another string against all substrings of one text
Need an online substring index
patterns.coreIdea: Build states that group substrings sharing the same occurrence-ending positions. Add characters using transitions, suffix links, and clones when needed; this compact structure represents all substrings.

patterns.name: Bitwise XOR
keywords: All values except one occur twice
Need to toggle an odd/even state
Need missing values or XOR comparisons under stated repetition rules
patterns.coreIdea: Use the fact that equal values XOR to zero and XOR with zero leaves a value unchanged. Track independent bits or parity; pair cancellation works only when the occurrence-count assumptions fit.

patterns.name: Bitmask Enumeration
keywords: A small set of items may be selected in any combination
Boolean choices fit in a mask
Need to test many subset compatibility rules
patterns.coreIdea: Use one bit per item to describe a subset, then try masks from zero through 2^n minus one. Bit operations test membership, but the number of subsets still grows exponentially.

patterns.name: Submask Enumeration
keywords: Split a chosen subset into smaller groups
Need all subsets contained in an allowed mask
A small-set DP chooses a whole group at once
patterns.coreIdea: To visit only subsets of a given mask, repeatedly use sub = (sub - 1) & mask. Handle the zero subset explicitly and stop there; visiting submasks of all masks takes O(3^n) total iterations.

patterns.name: Binary Lifting
keywords: Many kth-ancestor queries on the same tree
Repeatedly apply the same next-state function
Need fast jumps or ancestor comparisons after preprocessing
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute where 1, 2, 4, 8, and larger power-of-two jumps lead. Answer a long jump by combining its binary-sized pieces; tree-ancestor queries also need a clear missing-ancestor convention.

patterns.name: Fenwick Tree
keywords: Values change one position at a time
Need repeated prefix sums or frequency counts
Count earlier values by rank after coordinate compression
patterns.coreIdea: Store sums of selected power-of-two-sized ranges in an array. The lowest set bit tells which stored ranges a point update or prefix query must visit; range sums come from subtracting prefixes.
commonAlgorithms: Range update with dual Fenwick trees

patterns.name: Segment Tree
keywords: Need range sums, minima, or other summaries with updates
Input changes between queries
A query can combine answers from disjoint subranges
patterns.coreIdea: Divide the array into a tree of ranges and store a summary for each. Combine summaries to answer a query and update the ranges containing a changed position; the combining operation must be associative.

patterns.name: Lazy Segment Tree
keywords: Both updates and queries cover ranges
Increment or assign whole intervals
A valid update rule can modify a segment summary at once
patterns.coreIdea: Store pending range updates on segment-tree nodes and apply them to children only when needed. This works when update tags compose correctly and can transform a stored range summary without visiting every element.

patterns.name: Sparse Table
keywords: Many range-minimum or range-maximum queries
The array does not change
Combining an item with itself leaves the answer unchanged, as with min or GCD
patterns.coreIdea: Precompute summaries for ranges whose lengths are powers of two. On unchanged input, a minimum or other overlap-safe query can combine two covering blocks in constant time; sums need a different combination strategy.

patterns.name: Ordered Set
keywords: Need the next larger or smaller current value
Values arrive and leave online
Need sorted order, with special support if ranks or duplicates matter
patterns.coreIdea: Keep keys sorted while inserting, deleting, and finding neighboring values. Balanced search trees support this efficiently; Python's list plus bisect finds positions quickly but insertion and deletion are linear.

patterns.name: Strongly Connected Components
keywords: Dependencies contain directed cycles
Need groups of mutually reachable nodes
Collapsing cycles would simplify later graph processing
patterns.coreIdea: Group directed-graph nodes that can all reach one another. Replace each group by one node to obtain an acyclic graph; this separates cycles from the dependencies between groups.

patterns.name: Bridges
keywords: Removing one edge would split a connected component
Need critical network connections
Need to distinguish a bridge from an edge on a cycle
patterns.coreIdea: In an undirected DFS, track the earliest ancestor each child subtree can reach without its parent edge. That edge is a bridge if there is no alternate route back; parallel edges need separate edge identities.

patterns.name: Articulation Points
keywords: Removing one vertex would split a connected component
Need single points of failure
Need to identify articulation points rather than critical edges
patterns.coreIdea: In an undirected DFS, check whether a child subtree can reach above its parent without going through that parent. If not, removing the parent separates that branch; the DFS root has its own multiple-child rule.

patterns.name: Euler Tour
keywords: Many queries affect or summarize a subtree
Need ancestor checks from entry/exit times
Tree values can be flattened into DFS order
patterns.coreIdea: Assign DFS entry and exit positions so a node's entire subtree occupies one array range. This turns subtree sums or updates into range operations; path queries usually need additional structure.

patterns.name: Euler Path and Circuit
keywords: Reconstruct a route from tickets or directed pairs
Every connection must be used once
Vertices may repeat but edges may not
patterns.coreIdea: Find a route that uses every edge exactly once, not every vertex once. After checking degree and relevant connectivity conditions, follow unused edges and stitch the resulting trails together.

patterns.name: Maximum Flow
keywords: Connections have capacities
Need maximum transport or allocation
A matching or assignment can be modeled as units of flow
patterns.coreIdea: Send as much flow as possible from a source to a sink without exceeding edge capacities. Maintain reverse residual edges so later paths can undo and reroute earlier choices.

patterns.name: Minimum Cut
keywords: Need the cheapest capacity barrier between source and sink
Binary choices can be modeled by a cut
Vertex-removal costs can be transformed using node splitting
patterns.coreIdea: Separate a source from a sink by removing edges of minimum total capacity. After maximum flow, residual reachability identifies a minimum cut; a global cut without fixed endpoints is a different problem.

patterns.name: Bipartite Matching
keywords: Assign workers to jobs or people to resources
Each item can be matched at most once
Need the largest number of compatible left-right pairs
patterns.coreIdea: Split items into two sides and connect allowed pairs. Find one-to-one assignments by searching for paths that can rearrange existing matches and add another pair.

patterns.name: Greatest Common Divisor
keywords: Need the largest common divisor
Simplify a ratio or repeating unit
Combine divisibility periods through GCD and LCM
patterns.coreIdea: Repeatedly replace a pair of nonnegative integers (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b is zero. The remaining value is their greatest common divisor; use absolute values when inputs may be negative.

patterns.name: Modular Arithmetic
keywords: Answer is requested modulo a number
Only divisibility or remainder classes matter
Large counting formulas must stay within a modulus
patterns.coreIdea: Keep remainders when addition or multiplication would create huge values. Normalize signs according to the language; modular division requires an inverse and ordinary integer division is not a substitute.

patterns.name: Fast Power
keywords: Exponent is too large for repeated multiplication
Need modular powers
A repeated operation can be combined in power-of-two blocks
patterns.coreIdea: Build a power by repeatedly squaring the base and multiplying it into the answer for set bits of the exponent. This uses logarithmically many multiplications; apply the modulus at each step when needed.

patterns.name: Modular Inverse
keywords: Need division inside modular arithmetic
Compute factorial ratios under a prime modulus
Need to undo multiplication and the divisor is invertible
patterns.coreIdea: An inverse of a modulo m is a value that makes their product have remainder one. It exists exactly when a and m are coprime; use extended Euclid, or Fermat's exponent only under a prime modulus with a nonzero remainder.

patterns.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
keywords: Need all primes up to a known bound
Many primality queries share the same range
Many numbers need factorization after preprocessing
patterns.coreIdea: Build a table of primes up to a limit by marking multiples of each prime, starting at its square. A smallest-prime-factor table is a related preprocessing method for repeated factorizations.

patterns.name: Prime Factorization
keywords: Need divisor counts or prime exponents
Numbers are related by shared factors
Product or divisibility rules are easier to express with prime powers
patterns.coreIdea: Break a positive integer into prime factors and their counts. Trial division suits smaller single values; a precomputed smallest-prime-factor table helps when many bounded values must be factored.

patterns.name: Matrix Exponentiation
keywords: Need a recurrence value at a huge index
Each new state is a linear combination of a fixed number of earlier values
The same small transition matrix is reused many times
patterns.coreIdea: Write a fixed-size linear recurrence as one matrix transformation. Raise the transition matrix to a large power with repeated squaring instead of applying every intermediate step.

patterns.name: Combinatorics
keywords: Choose items or arrange positions
Count interleavings or repeated objects
Direct enumeration is too large and the structure can be counted
patterns.coreIdea: Decide what distinguishes an outcome before counting it: order, repetition, and overlap all matter. Then choose a formula or recurrence such as combinations, permutations, or inclusion-exclusion.

patterns.name: Catalan Numbers
keywords: Count balanced-parenthesis sequences
Count binary-tree shapes or polygon triangulations
Noncrossing structures split into two independent smaller structures
patterns.coreIdea: Look for objects that split into an independent left part and right part around a root or matching pair. Summing the products of the two smaller counts gives Catalan's recurrence, with the empty object counted as one.
